Treating cancer pain in dogs and cats (https://www.dvm360.com/view/treating-cancer-pain-dogs-and-cats)
【turn1052search0】 [wordlim: 200] Published: today; Crawled: today; Content type: text/html; 9 hours ago — The goal in managing dogs and cats with cancer is to control pain and improve a patient's overall quality of life by using traditional anticancer therapeutic ... Read more
Pain frequently accompanies cancer in people and is also common in cancer-bearing dogs and cats. Pain negatively affects quality of life and important physiological functions, and eliminating it should be a priority. Whether cancer pain has been identified, is suspected, or is expected to occur in a cancer-bearing patient, efforts should be directed at treating and preventing it effectively. While pain in certain dogs and cats with cancer will be relieved with treatment directed toward the underlying cancer, others will require symptomatic analgesic therapy to improve their quality of life. A relative abundance of literature discusses the management of cancer pain in people.1-7 In contrast, there is a paucity of information specifically regarding the management of veterinary cancer pain. Recent publications, ongoing prospective studies, and better knowledge of the available therapeutic options should provide the necessary framework for appropriate pain management in cancer-bearing pets.8-14

### METHODS OF PAIN RELIEF FOR CANCER PATIENTS

The most rational way to alleviate cancer pain, whenever possible, is to treat the underlying tumor. Always evaluate the possibility of surgically removing a resectable tumor or obtaining a remission by using radiation therapy for a radiosensitive tumor or chemotherapy for a chemosensitive cancer. While you are waiting for the definitive therapy to take effect and eliminate the source of pain, analgesic and supportive therapies are often required to improve a patient's quality of life. And occasionally, with resistant, refractory, recurring, or terminal cancers, only palliative therapy can truly benefit a patient.

The goal in managing dogs and cats with cancer is to control pain and improve a patient's overall quality of life by using traditional anticancer therapeutic modalities, various analgesic therapies, and supportive care. Before you treat for cancer pain, you must have a basic understanding of the pathophysiology of pain and of the methods used to recognize and evaluate pain in veterinary patients (see the article "Understanding and recognizing cancer pain in dogs and cats").

### TREATMENT DIRECTED AT THE TUMOR

### Surgery

Whenever possible, completely remove a painful tumor surgically. With an appropriate preemptive and multimodal analgesic program in place, including postoperative pain management, most patients with tumors causing pain will be more comfortable after radical surgeries. Surgery is the modality that can most rapidly eliminate the source of pain, and various surgical procedures can be performed, depending on the tumor's type, extent, and location. Examples of tumors best treated and possibly cured with surgery alone include canine oral tumors such as squamous cell carcinoma and fibrosarcoma, cutaneous mast cell tumors, mammary tumors, soft tissue sarcomas, splenic or hepatic tumors with painful capsular distention, nail bed tumors, synovial cell sarcoma causing bone lysis, and tumors of the ear canal.

Occasionally, patients will benefit from palliative surgeries to remove painful tumors, although the surgery itself may not positively affect the overall prognosis for survival. A classic example is a painful appendicular osteosarcoma in which metastatic disease ultimately determines the survival time. In this example, amputating the limb provides immediate relief to the patient, and adjuvant chemotherapy is administered to prolong survival and delay the growth of micrometastatic disease.

Studying STING therapy in canine sarcoma patients provides a unique opportunity to explore a clinically translational animal model that recapitulates tumor size and clinical progression of human disease. Methods: Four sarcoma-bearing dogs were recruited for this study. All subjects underwent weekly intratumoral STING therapy until a surgical or humane-endpoints were reached. Tumor volume, vital signs, and weight were measured at each visit. Two STING agonists were studied (ADU-S100 – CDN and E7766). Sera were collected prior to and 6h following STING immunotherapy to measure systemic cytokine levels. Histologic assessment of tumors was completed at time of biopsy or necropsy. Results: All dogs experienced a reduction in tumor volume. Two dogs became surgical candidates following STING treatment. Overall survival varied between 14-736 days among treated dogs. Systemic cytokine elevation was observed following STING therapy. At time of necropsy, none of the dogs showed macroscopic evidence of metastatic disease. Conclusions: Intralesional STING immunotherapy is a feasible treatment for dogs with sarcoma, demonstrating biological activity enabling surgical intervention in 2/4 dogs. At time of necropsy, no metastatic disease was observed. Future prospective cohort studies should be completed to further investigate this translational immunotherapy.

# Infections linked to one in eight cancers

4 minute read

Infectious disease oncology Public Health Research

* * *

Image

By

Amanda Sheppeard

Image

Some 2.3 million cancer cases worldwide were attributable to infections in 2024, with five pathogens accounting for almost all cases and low- and middle-income countries bearing the greatest burden.

* * *

Infections caused an estimated 12% of all cancers diagnosed worldwide in 2024, highlighting major opportunities for cancer prevention through vaccination, screening, and treatment, according to new research.

The global analysis, published in The Lancet Oncology, was led by researchers at the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC).

They found that about 2.3 million new cancer cases were attributable to infectious agents, with Helicobacter pylori and human papillomavirus (HPV) responsible for almost two-thirds of the burden.

“Previous global estimates indicated that approximately 2.2 million cancers worldwide were attributable to infections in 2018, with the highest burden in eastern Asia and sub-Saharan Africa,” the researchers wrote.

“These estimates have informed prevention strategies but, since then, evidence has strengthened on carcinogenicity for additional infectious agents not previously considered (notably HIV and Merkel cell polyomavirus [MCV]) and on causal associations between established Group 1 infectious agents and additional cancer types, such as Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) and gastric cancer.”

The researchers assessed 12 infectious agents classified as carcinogenic to humans, combining GLOBOCAN 2024 cancer incidence estimates with population-attributable fractions for 37 established infection–cancer associations.

H. pylori accounted for the largest number of cases, with an estimated 760,000 cancers, or 4% of all new cancer diagnoses globally.

Human papillomavirus (HPV) followed closely with 750,000 cases (4%), while hepatitis B virus (HBV) accounted for 360,000 cases (2%), EBV for 260,000 cases (1%), and hepatitis C virus (HCV) for 160,000 cases (<1%).

The findings revealed substantial geographical inequalities, with low- and middle-income countries accounting for 77% of infection-attributable cancers.

Eastern Asia recorded the greatest absolute burden, with approximately 990,000 cases, representing 42% of the global total. The region’s burden was predominantly driven by H. pylori, responsible for 410,000 cases, and HBV, which accounted for 260,000 cases.

Sub-Saharan Africa had the highest proportion of cancers attributable to infections, at 25% of all new diagnoses, compared with the global average of 12%. HPV was the leading contributor in the region, accounting for approximately 130,000 cases, or 14% of all cancers diagnosed there.

By comparison, infections accounted for 8% of cancers in high-income countries and 5% in Oceania, where approximately 11,000 infection-attributable cancers were estimated in 2024.

The global age-standardised incidence rate for infection-attributable cancers was 22.7 per 100,000 person-years, rising to 31.9 in eastern Asia and 28.5 in sub-Saharan Africa. Oceania recorded a rate of 16.7 per 100,000.

The analysis also identified marked differences in the cancer types associated with individual pathogens.

Of the 760,000 cancers attributable to H. pylori, approximately 700,000 were non-cardia gastric cancers, representing 85% of all cancers diagnosed at that site.

HPV was responsible for an estimated 600,000 cervical cancers, as well as 58,000 oropharyngeal cancers and 32,000 anal squamous cell carcinomas.

HBV and HCV were predominantly associated with hepatocellular carcinoma, accounting for approximately 330,000 and 130,000 cases respectively.

EBV was linked to a broader range of malignancies, including 110,000 nasopharyngeal cancers, 78,000 gastric cancers, and 47,000 cases of Hodgkin lymphoma.

# Nestlé supports global effort to improve nutritional care in cancer surgery

Oct 15, 2026

Nestlé supports global effort to improve nutritional care in cancer surgery

In brief 

  * Nestlé is supporting the World Society of Surgical Oncology (WSSO) to develop expert recommendations on nutritional care for patients undergoing cancer surgery. 
  * Up to 70% of cancer patients may be malnourished, depending on the type and stage of cancer. 
  * A global panel of 15 medical experts will review the evidence and develop practical recommendations, expected in the second half of 2027.

Nestlé will support the World Society of Surgical Oncology (WSSO) in an international initiative to develop expert recommendations on nutritional care for patients undergoing cancer surgery. The aim is to build a more consistent approach to nutrition in surgical cancer care and encourage healthcare systems to identify patients at nutritional risk and provide appropriate support.

Malnutrition is an often-overlooked issue in cancer treatment. Studies suggest that up to 70% of cancer patients may be malnourished or at risk of malnutrition, depending on tumor type and clinical context.^{1} Malnutrition can also increase healthcare costs, with studies showing substantially higher costs for malnourished patients.^{2}

Appropriate nutritional support before an operation can reduce the risk of complications and infections as well as the length of hospital stays and unplanned readmissions. An analysis of 56 trials found that providing nutritional support before surgery reduced complications and shortened hospital stays.^{3}

"This global initiative can help put nutrition where it belongs: at the centre of cancer surgery," said Dr. Sara Colombo Mottaz, Pharm PhD (Doctor of Philosophy), Head of Medical, Scientific and Regulatory Affairs Unit at Nestlé. "By improving diagnosis for malnutrition and providing the right nutritional support, we can help achieve better outcomes for patients while helping to reduce pressure on healthcare systems."

The first-of-its-kind panel will bring together 15 medical experts from around the world, spanning surgery, nursing, anesthesia and dietetics. The independent panel will review the latest scientific evidence and develop practical recommendations to help integrate nutrition more systematically into the care of cancer patients undergoing surgery.

"We know that nutritional care can contribute to better outcomes for patients undergoing cancer surgery, but it is not yet consistently part of surgical care," said Dr. Rodrigo Pinheiro from the World Society of Surgical Oncology. "Through this collaboration, we aim to help translate the evidence into practical recommendations that can improve care for patients worldwide."

The panel's conclusions and recommendations are expected in the second half of 2027. They will be shared with healthcare professionals, policymakers and governments to raise awareness and recommend adoption of evidence-based nutritional practices in cancer care.

* * *

^{1} BMC Cancer. 2025 / ESPEN. 2025
^{2} A study in the UK (United Kingdom) found that managing a malnourished patient costs GBP (Great British Pound)1 753 vs GBP (Great British Pound)750 over six months. (Guest et al, 2011)

## Principles of apSTAR

The two principles underlying apSTAR are: local destruction of tumor by means of a laser combined with a photo-absorbing dye and stimulated immune response due to the application of an immunoadjuvant, but also due to increases in antigen accessibility caused by the destruction of the tumor. Both elements of this protocol are crucial. Since this method independently triggers the immune response in each individual, it does not depend upon cross reactivity in the expression of tumor-specific antigen between hosts (as is required in conventional antibody immunotherapy and vaccination.)

## Durée des études

### Phase de recherche pré-clinique

Avant de lancer un essai clinique de médicament, environ médicaments potentiels ont été testés en laboratoire sur des cellules et des animaux. Les nouvelles molécules potentiellement intéressantes en termes pharmacologiques doivent d'abord être découvertes (l'intelligence artificielle peut grandement accélérer cette phase), purifiées, caractérisées et testées en laboratoire (sur des cellules et des animaux) avant de passer aux essais cliniques. Pour un médicament contre le cancer, en moyenne six ans sont nécessaires pour cette phase préparatoire.

Le premier obstacle à la réalisation des études est souvent le manque de participants adéquats et volontaires généralement bénévoles qui savent qu'ils recevront peut-être un placebo ou au moins un médicament dont l'efficacité n'est pas encore prouvée. Tous les essais de médicaments et de nombreux essais de dispositifs ciblent un sous-ensemble particulier de la population, et certains essais cliniques nécessitent des patients présentant des spécificités génétiques ou des combinaisons inhabituelles de caractéristiques de la maladie. Cela doit se faire dans une base de données accessible sur internet : ClinicalTrials.gov. À partir de septembre 2008, le dossier des études devra être enrichi des résultats obtenus, dans un délai d'un an après l'intervention auprès du dernier « sujet ». Cette base contient plus de études faites dans plus de (30 % proviennent d'en dehors des États-Unis).

En parallèle, l'industrie pharmaceutique américaine alimente une autre base de données, également accessible par internet, contenant le résultat des études cliniques réalisées pour les médicaments sur le marché.

Les Instituts de recherche en santé du Canada demandent pour leur part l'enregistrement auprès de « Current Controlled Trials », qui attribue un International Standard Randomised Controlled Trial Number (ISRCTN).

Comme les registres se multiplient, l'Organisation mondiale de la santé les a regroupés dans son système d'enregistrement international des essais cliniques, qui se veut la porte d'entrée pour tous les essais en cours dans le monde entier.

## Career and research

LeBlanc was an associate professor with tenure and director of translational research at the University of Tennessee College of Veterinary Medicine (CVM) and University of Tennessee College of Medicine. LeBlanc's group at the University of Tennessee published the first comprehensive studies describing molecular imaging of dogs and cats using PET-CT, focusing on the forward and back-translation of 18F-labelled radiopharmaceuticals.

LeBlanc is a board-certified veterinary oncologist and senior scientist in the molecular imaging program at the National Cancer Institute (NCI). She is director of the NCI's Comparative Oncology Program. Her research focus is in animal modeling for development of new cancer drugs and imaging agents, and identification of imaging biomarkers, development and optimization of PET imaging hardware and imaging protocols. In her position, she oversees and manages the operations of the Comparative Oncology Trials Consortium (COTC), which designs and executes clinical trials of new cancer therapies in tumor-bearing pet dogs.

Veterinary oncology
Cancer diagnosis and treatment in animals

Veterinary oncology is a subspecialty of veterinary medicine that deals with cancer diagnosis and treatment in animals. Cancer is a major cause of death in pet animals. In one study, 45% of the dogs that reached 10 years of age or older died of cancer.

Skin tumors are the most frequently diagnosed type of tumor in domestic animals for two reasons: 1. constant exposure of animal skin to the sun and external environment, 2. skin tumors are easy to see because they are on the outside of the animal.

## History

Specialised veterinary oncology training became available in the 21st century.
## Treatment

The most effective method of treating cancer in animals is surgery. Surgery may involve a marginal excision, where just the capsule is excised; wide excision, where a wider area surrounding the capsule (typically 2–3cm) is excised; or radical excision, where the entire compartment is excised, often taking the form of an amputation.

【turn1052academia17】 [wordlim: 200] Published: 6 days ago; 
Title: Documenting Trofinetide Treatment Phenotypes in Rett Syndrome with a Dual-LLM Consensus Pipeline
Authors: Daniel Palacios, Guantong Qi, Mikael Guzman Karlsson, Shawntel K. David, Mohammed Sameeruddin, Bernhard Suter, Zhandong Liu, Davut Pehlivan, Hu Chen
Date: Thu Oct 15 15:24:47 2026

Objective: Trofinetide, approved in 2023 as the first Rett syndrome treatment, lacks scalable real-world monitoring because chart review is labor-intensive. We developed a dual large language model (LLM) consensus pipeline to extract 18 treatment-response phenotypes, comprising 4 adverse effects, 13 Rett clinical features, and medication refusal, from clinical notes. Materials and Methods: We analyzed 26,763 notes from 108 patients with confirmed sustained trofinetide exposure at Texas Children's Hospital. The pipeline filters notes by keyword, classifies each through two LLMs requiring consensus, and aggregates a patient-by-timepoint matrix. Architecture and prompt were selected on a diarrhea development set, then frozen and applied to the other 17 phenotypes with the phenotype definition substituted, as an out-of-sample test. The reported prompt comparison scores 183 expert-labeled cells. Results: A prompt requiring diarrhea to be active and severe performed best (84.2 $\pm$ 0.0% accuracy; F1 = 0.674), 47 percentage points above regular-expression matching ($p < 0.0001$). Expert reviewers judged six of the pipeline's calls per phenotype, three positive and three negative, and agreed with 90.2% (92/102). The 13 Rett clinical features are manifestations of the disorder itself rather than adverse effects of trofinetide. Gross and fine motor impairment, language/communication, and stereotypy were documented present in 92-100% of patients at every visit. Discussion: In-context LLM extraction captured multi-domain treatment responses. The outcome is documented presence at each visit, not a direction-of-change judgment. Conclusion: Coupling in-context LLM reasoning with a consensus architecture offers a scalable alternative to keyword and regular-expression extraction for real-world evidence, adapting to new phenotypes and medications through configuration alone.

Trial design considerations in the face of overdispersion and time-varying event rates: a meta-regression approach with an application in asthma (https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21432)
【turn1052academia18】 [wordlim: 200] Published: 6 days ago; 
Title: Trial design considerations in the face of overdispersion and time-varying event rates: a meta-regression approach with an application in asthma
Authors: Bohua Chen, Christian Röver, Stefan Andreas, Christian Taube, Tim Friede
Date: Thu Oct 15 07:44:40 2026

**Purpose:** Relative changes in event rates are a common primary endpoint in confirmatory asthma trials. Reliable assumptions about baseline event rates and extra-Poisson variability are essential for sample size planning. We synthesize placebo-group exacerbation data, evaluate calendar-time trends, and assess implications for trial design. **Methods:** We systematically reviewed randomized controlled trials reporting recurrent asthma exacerbations and extracted control-group outcomes classified by placebo type or asthma severity. Hierarchical negative binomial models accommodated heterogeneous reporting formats and jointly modeled event rates and overdispersion. We compared separate subgroup models with covariate-based models and used meta-regression to adjust for calendar-time trends. Trial design implications were illustrated using the NAVIGATOR trial. **Results:** Sixty-two trials met the inclusion criteria. The estimated relative change in annualized exacerbation rates was -1.8% per year (95% CrI: -7.5%, 4.3%), corresponding to a 16.5% decrease per decade (95% CrI: -54.2%, 52.2%). Substantial between-study heterogeneity in event rates and overdispersion was observed. Within-trial overdispersion was estimated as 1.53 (95% CrI: 0.60, 2.83). In an illustrative phase III design scenario, sample size requirements were sensitive to the target subgroup and uncertainty in the predicted event rate and overdispersion. **Conclusion:** Event rates in clinical trials exhibit considerable heterogeneity and potential temporal variation, and overdispersion is a critical design parameter. Comprehensive modelling of recurrent-event endpoints allows for evidence-based and robust sample size calculations and trial design.

SurvICL: a Foundation Model for in-context Survival Analysis (https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22242)
【turn1052academia19】 [wordlim: 200] Published: 6 days ago; 
Title: SurvICL: a Foundation Model for in-context Survival Analysis
Authors: Julie Alberge, Linus Bleistein, Judith Abécassis, Marine Le Morvan, Gaël Varoquaux, David Holzmüller
Date: Thu Oct 15 17:16:56 2026

Tabular foundation models (TFMs) now outperform gradient-boosted trees in classification and regression. Yet in survival analysis, which predicts when an event occurs from censored data, often on small clinical cohorts, we find that no existing TFM beats the half-century-old Cox model. We address this issue by introducing SurvICL, a TFM that predicts survival curves in-context. SurvICL is pretrained on purely synthetic datasets generated from a novel flexible proportional-odds prior that outperforms other prior types in our ablation study. Unlike most other survival models, SurvICL is trained with a plain quantile regression loss, which is possible because its synthetic pre-training data generator can provide uncensored event times. Additionally, we introduce the largest survival benchmark to date spanning 103 datasets. On the 63 datasets held out from all design decisions, SurvICL outperforms 20 tree-based, deep, and foundation-model baselines without any tuning: it wins 82.9\% of pairwise comparisons in integrated Brier score, against 71.3\% for the runner-up, the Cox model, and is the first model to rank above Cox on small datasets.

Title: Pathology foundation models for training-free case retrieval in salivary gland tumors

In pathology, pattern recognition relies on a frame of reference built through extensive training and experience, which may still fall short when encountering rare cancer subtypes. Archives of previously diagnosed tumors often contain relevant precedents, yet identifying the most relevant cases remains challenging. Here we explore whether content-based retrieval with current pathology foundation models facilitates rare cancer diagnostics without any task-specific training. Pathologists can query a digitized archive using a region of interest (ROI) from a whole slide image (WSI) and retrieve morphologically similar cases, along with their ICD-O codes and corresponding WSIs. The ROI can be selected manually or automatically using a gated attention-based multiple instance learning model. We evaluate our approach by leave-one-case-out on an imbalanced dataset of 137 salivary gland tumor cases spanning 12 ICD-O morphology categories, comparing four pathology foundation models (Atlas2, Atlas2-B, Atlas2-S, and UNI2h). Top-1/3/5 retrieval was 62.5%/76.7%/81.3% for Atlas2, 50.2/66.6/72.9% for UNI2h, 52.3%/71.5%/77.6% for Atlas2-B and 54.4/65.2/73.7% for Atlas2-S. Macro-averaged F1 ranged from 69.0% for the smallest model Atlas2-S to 76.6% for the largest model Atlas2 across the five classes with at least ten cases. Our modified Chamfer similarity separated correct from incorrect matches among the Top-5 more reliably for Atlas2 (AUC 0.754) than for Atlas2-B (0.679, p = 0.020) and Atlas2-S (0.653, p = 0.003), but not UNI2h (0.697, p = 0.196). Requiring no additional training or manual annotation, this approach makes departmental archives searchable with pathology foundation models, providing a low-barrier route to case-based differential diagnosis and extending the individual frame of reference to the collective experience of the department.
